entries.content: Always end code blocks with ``` on its own line. Never use ellipsis (...) in code.

* * Check API docs with `apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(app_name, api_name)` before calling any API. TRUNCATION CHECK: If the output ends with `[TRUNCATED]` or cuts off mid-text, you did NOT read the full doc. Re-request by printing only the specific field you need — e.g., `doc = apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(...); print([(p['name'], p['description']) for p in doc['parameters']])`. Never assume parameter semantics from names alone when the full doc was not read. HARD BLOCK FOR PARTITION LOGIC: If you plan to use a filter parameter (e.g., `user_email`, `query`, `owner`, `type`) to CATEGORIZE items into different operation buckets (create vs. update, include vs. exclude), you MUST read its FULL non-truncated parameter description first. A misunderstood filter silently produces the wrong partition — even when the final state looks correct.
Write small, incremental code chunks - verify each step works before proceeding.
Use `supervisor` app for account credentials: `apis.supervisor.show_account_passwords()`

* HARD RULE — IDENTITY RESOLUTION: WHENEVER a task filters actions by person identity (friends, contacts, people you know, colleagues, family), you MUST resolve identities through phone contacts FIRST: `apis.phone.search_contacts(access_token=token, query=name)`. Phone contacts are the CANONICAL source of 'who you know.' NEVER use a platform's own friend/follower list (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_friends`, Spotify followers) as the sole identity source — platform friend lists may include or exclude different people than your phone contacts. Always: (1) Log into phone app, (2) Fetch all phone contacts, (3) Map each contact to the target platform by searching with their email/name, (4) Use ONLY the mapped set for filtering.

Variables persist across code blocks — reuse them instead of re-fetching. CRITICAL: Never use `apis` as a loop variable, assignment target, or parameter name (e.g., `for app, apis in dict.items()` will destroy the framework object permanently). Use names like `api_names`, `app_apis`, `api_list` instead.
Paginated APIs require looping: `while True: page = api(page_index=i); if not page: break`
Example credentials shown in few-shot examples are FAKE - always fetch real credentials from supervisor.

Always call `apis.supervisor.complete_task()` when done - this marks the task complete. Only pass an `answer=` argument if the task explicitly asks you to find, calculate, or return a specific value. For action-only tasks (e.g., 'send a message', 'play a song'), call `complete_task()` with NO answer argument.

* Before any bulk action (approve, delete, send, modify), explicitly extract ALL filtering criteria from BOTH the task instruction AND any referenced conversation context (text messages, emails the task refers to). Conversation content defines binding requirements — a request asking for 'movies by director X' means ONLY those movies, not all movies. Build a target set by cross-referencing relevant data sources. Print the target set and its count. Only act on entities in that set — never default to 'all'. EQUALLY CRITICAL: Do NOT add filtering criteria the task does not specify. If you compute a target set of N items, you must act on all N — never skip items based on self-invented 'smart' checks.

MISTAKE: Approving/deleting/modifying ALL matching entities when the task specifies a filtered subset (e.g., 'approve requests from my contacts' ≠ 'approve all requests'). FIX: Re-read the task instruction, identify qualifier words (from contacts, under $50, from last week, etc.), and build the filtered target set BEFORE acting.

Cross-referencing workflow for filtered actions: (1) Fetch primary entities (e.g., payment requests). (2) Identify filtering source from task (e.g., phone contacts, specific people). (3) Log into and fetch data from the filtering source. (4) Compute intersection to get target IDs. (5) Print target IDs for verification. (6) Execute action ONLY on target IDs.

PRE-COMPLETION GATE: Before calling complete_task, list every app/API you explored (looked up docs, listed endpoints). If you explored an app's docs but never called its data APIs, STOP and either use it or write an explicit justification why it's irrelevant. Abandoning an explored data source almost always means you skipped a required identity resolution or filtering step.

Bulk irreversible actions need try/except per item to maintain control:
```
results = []
for eid in target_ids:
    try:
        r = apis.app.action(id=eid, access_token=token)
        results.append((eid, 'ok', r))
    except Exception as e:
        results.append((eid, 'fail', str(e)))
print('succeeded:', [r for r in results if r[1]=='ok'])
print('failed:', [r for r in results if r[1]=='fail'])
```

When an error occurs mid-bulk-operation (e.g., insufficient balance), fix only HOW to perform the action (e.g., add payment card), not WHAT to act on. Re-derive the target set from original filtering criteria — don't just re-fetch 'remaining' items, as some may have already been processed and the remaining set no longer matches the original filter.

* * Cross-platform identity resolution procedure — MANDATORY when task involves people from contacts on another platform (Venmo, Gmail, Spotify, etc.): (1) Log into phone app and fetch ALL contacts (`apis.phone.search_contacts`). (2) For EACH contact, search for their account on the target platform using their email (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_users(query=email)`). Do NOT skip verification — if 0 results, email may not match. (3) Build target person set ONLY from successfully resolved contacts. (4) Cross-check: resolved account name should match phone contact name. CRITICAL: Do NOT substitute platform-native friend lists (e.g., `search_friends`, `show_followers`) for this procedure — they represent a DIFFERENT social graph than your phone contacts and will produce wrong target sets.

* After bulk record creation (payment requests, messages, orders): (1) Verify COUNT of actions taken equals COUNT of originally computed target set. If fewer, identify every exclusion and confirm it's justified by the task text — not self-invented logic. (2) Fetch back the created records and compare (recipient_id/email, amount/content) pairs against your computed expected set. Print both sets side by side. Flag and fix any mismatches before calling complete_task.

MISTAKE: Using `apis` as a loop/comprehension variable (e.g., `for app, apis in explored.items():`) which permanently overwrites the framework ApiCollection object with a plain list/string. Once overwritten, the session is UNRECOVERABLE — you cannot reconstruct the ApiCollection. FIX: Never reuse the name `apis` for any purpose other than the framework object. Use `api_list`, `api_names`, `app_apis`, `items`, etc.

SUDDEN TOTAL API FAILURE: If all `apis.*` calls that previously worked start returning the same error (e.g., `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'supervisor'` or `HTTPException 422`), the most likely cause is that `apis` was accidentally overwritten by your own code. Diagnostic: (1) Run `print(type(apis))` — expect `ApiCollection`, NOT `list`/`str`/`dict`. (2) If overwritten, do NOT spend steps trying to recover — it is unrecoverable. (3) Instead, verify whether the task actions were already completed before the corruption, and report completion if so.

RECOVERY BUDGET LIMIT: If 3 consecutive attempts to fix a broken state all fail with the same error pattern, STOP retrying. Either (a) pivot to a fundamentally different approach, or (b) if the core task actions were already completed, attempt `complete_task()` one final time and move on. Never spend more than 5 steps on recovery from a single failure mode.

* ANSWER FORMAT GATE: Before calling `complete_task(answer=...)`, re-read the exact task instruction. (1) Identify the precise question phrasing: 'how much did I send?' → single dollar amount, 'what is the difference?' → net value, 'how many?' → integer count. (2) Format the answer as the most concise value that directly answers that question — typically a single number, name, or short phrase. (3) Do NOT include labels, multiple values, or explanatory text unless the question explicitly requests them. (4) If the task asks one question but you computed multiple values, pick only the one that answers the question asked.

MISTAKE: Using API filter parameters like `direction='sent'`/`direction='received'` or `type`/`role` without verifying what perspective they represent. FIX: After the first API call with a direction/type/role parameter, print at least one full returned record. Verify the interpretation matches your assumption (e.g., confirm `direction='sent'` + `user_email=X` returns transactions where YOU sent money TO X, not vice versa). A wrong interpretation silently swaps or misattributes totals.

* MISTAKE: Over-filtering by inventing criteria the task never specified — e.g., computing 4 unpaid people but then skipping one because a pending request already exists for them (from a different context). This silently drops required actions. FIX: Use ONLY the filtering criteria stated in the task. 'Has not paid' means no completed payment/transaction found — NOT 'has no pending request.' Never add deduplication, idempotency, or 'already handled' checks unless the task explicitly requires them.

* Request-fulfillment from conversations workflow: When a task involves responding to or fulfilling a request found in text messages or emails: (1) Fetch the COMPLETE conversation thread with the requester (use `show_text_message_window` or paginate `search_text_messages` filtered by their phone number — do NOT rely on truncated search results). (2) Read ALL messages from the requester to extract their EXACT ask, including any qualifiers (specific director, genre, price range, date, quantity, etc.). (3) Write out the extracted criteria explicitly as an intermediate artifact before proceeding. (4) Fetch source data (notes, lists, etc.) and apply ALL extracted filters. (5) Before sending the response, verify: the items included match the filtered set, NOT the full unfiltered source.

* MISTAKE: When a task says 'reply to X's request' or 'send X what they asked for', composing the response from ALL available source data without reading the full conversation to understand what X specifically asked for. This silently sends unfiltered data when X requested a filtered subset. FIX: Always fetch and read the COMPLETE conversation thread BEFORE composing any response. The requester's messages contain implicit filtering criteria (e.g., 'by this director', 'under $50', 'from last month') that are just as binding as explicit task instructions. Never assume 'send everything' — verify the exact scope of the request.

* MISTAKE: When exporting/backing up data, progressively collecting from ALL available data endpoints (song library → album library → playlist library → liked playlists) without pre-defining scope. Progressive accumulation creates commitment bias — after collecting from 4 sources and reaching 90 items vs 12 from the primary source, the inflated result 'feels normal' and is never questioned. FIX: BEFORE collecting, print a scope table mapping each endpoint to IN/OUT based on the task's exact wording. 'Song library' = show_song_library endpoint ONLY — albums and playlists are SEPARATE collections. HARD TRIGGER: If you find yourself calling more than one *_library endpoint, STOP and verify each additional source is explicitly requested by the task.

* MANDATORY scope definition workflow (export/backup/collection tasks) — execute BEFORE collecting ANY data: (1) List ALL available data endpoints for the platform (e.g., show_song_library, show_album_library, show_playlist_library, show_liked_playlists). (2) Print a SCOPE TABLE: for each endpoint, write IN-SCOPE or OUT-OF-SCOPE with justification tied to the task's EXACT wording. DEFAULT to narrowest interpretation: 'song library' → show_song_library ONLY; 'library' → show_*_library endpoints; 'all account data' → everything. Liked/followed/recommended content is OUT unless explicitly requested. (3) Collect ONLY from in-scope endpoints. PROGRESSIVE SIZE GATE: After adding each new source, compare total unique items to the primary source count. If total exceeds 2× the primary source, STOP immediately and re-read the task — you are almost certainly over-expanding scope. (4) Print final item count and scope justification before writing any output file.

DATA SCOPE GATE (for export/backup tasks): Before writing the output artifact, list each data source endpoint used and its record count. For each source, confirm the task's wording includes it — don't assume 'library' means 'everything on the platform.' If total records vastly exceed the primary source count, treat as a red flag for over-expansion and re-verify scope against the task text before proceeding.

* MISTAKE: Using a platform's own friend/social list (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_friends()`, Spotify followers) as the identity source when the task says 'contacts' or 'friends' or 'people I know.' Platform friend lists are NOT equivalent to phone contacts — they may include strangers added on-platform and exclude real contacts who aren't platform friends. This silently produces wrong target sets. FIX: ALWAYS resolve identity through `apis.phone.search_contacts()` first, then map each phone contact to the target platform. If you find yourself calling a platform's friend/follower API as your FIRST identity step, STOP — you're using the wrong source.

* IDENTITY SOURCE GATE: Before executing any bulk action filtered by person identity, verify and print: (1) Identity source used — must be phone contacts, NOT a platform-native friend list. (2) Number of phone contacts resolved. (3) Number successfully mapped to target platform accounts. (4) Final target entity IDs derived from this mapping. If you used a platform friend list without consulting phone contacts, STOP and redo identity resolution through phone contacts before proceeding.

Superlative query resolution workflow — when the task asks for the 'most,' 'least,' 'highest,' 'lowest,' 'best,' or 'worst' of something over a dataset: (1) Fetch ALL relevant data (paginate fully). (2) Identify the entity being ranked (artist, person, item) and the metric. (3) If no explicit score/rating field exists in the data, default to FREQUENCY-BASED counting (e.g., 'least recommended artist' = artist with fewest songs in recommendations). (4) NEVER assume API list position equals ranking unless the API docs explicitly state the ordering criterion — check docs for `sort_by`, `order`, or ordering description. (5) Perform explicit aggregation: group by entity, compute the metric (count/sum/avg), sort, extract the superlative. (6) Print the full ranked table as an intermediate artifact before answering. (7) Sanity-check: if your chosen answer also appears at the opposite extreme (e.g., same artist at position 1 and last position), your interpretation is wrong — recompute.

MISTAKE: Treating API list position as a ranking (e.g., assuming the last item in a recommendations list is 'least recommended'). API response ordering is NOT a reliable proxy for ranking unless the docs explicitly state it. FIX: For any superlative query ('most/least X'), compute the answer explicitly by aggregating across ALL returned data — count occurrences, sum values, etc. Before submitting, verify your interpretation is self-consistent: if the same entity appears at both the top and bottom of the list, positional ordering is clearly not the ranking criterion.

* EXPORT FILE READBACK GATE: After writing an output file for export/backup tasks, ALWAYS read the file back and verify BEFORE completing the task or deleting source data/accounts. Check: (1) Record count matches the expected in-scope count from your scope table. (2) Sample 3-5 entries and compare against raw API data for correctness. (3) Multi-value fields (multiple artists, tags) use an appropriate format. CRITICAL: Never delete a source account until the backup file has been read back and verified — deletion is irreversible and prevents recovery from export errors.

MISTAKE: Using a search/filter API parameter (e.g., `user_email`, `query`, `owner`) for existence detection in bulk operations without validating it actually filters correctly. The parameter might search text content instead of matching record ownership, silently return empty due to format mismatches, or filter on a different field than assumed. This causes wrong categorization of items into create vs. update buckets. FIX: Before relying on any filter parameter for bulk categorization: (1) Read the FULL (non-truncated) API doc for that parameter. (2) For 2-3 items where the filter returns results, also fetch ALL records for that entity (unfiltered) and confirm the filtered results are a correct subset. (3) For 1-2 items where the filter returns empty, confirm via unfiltered fetch that no matching record truly exists. If validation fails, switch to unfiltered fetching + manual matching in code.

* * PARTITION VERIFICATION GATE (for bulk add/update/skip operations): When a task requires splitting items into different operation types (create new vs. update existing, approve vs. reject): (1) VALIDATE the detection method BEFORE executing — for 2+ items per bucket, fetch ALL records UNFILTERED for that entity and manually confirm your categorization matches. If you used a filter parameter (e.g., `user_email`) to detect existence, compare filtered results against the full unfiltered set for those same items. If any mismatch, switch to unfiltered fetch + code-level matching. (2) Print a partition summary table BEFORE executing: `create: [ids...] (N), update: [ids...] (M), skip: [ids...] (K)`. (3) AFTER execution, verify BOTH final state AND operation correctness. Final-state-only verification (e.g., 'all ratings are now 5') is INSUFFICIENT — the evaluation may validate WHICH items were created vs. updated, not just the end result. For 'created' records, confirm no prior record existed; for 'updated' records, confirm the review_id existed before.

* PARTITION-CRITICAL DETECTION — PREFER UNFILTERED FETCH + CODE MATCHING: When categorizing items into create vs. update buckets and the dataset is small (< 100 items), do NOT rely solely on API filter parameters (e.g., `user_email`, `query`) to detect whether your record exists. Instead: (1) Fetch ALL records for each entity UNFILTERED (e.g., `show_song_reviews(song_id=X)` with no user_email param). (2) Inspect returned record fields (user_id, email, username) to find YOUR record via code-level matching. (3) Categorize create vs. update based on this manual match. API filter parameters may search text content, match partial strings, or filter on a different field than assumed — silently producing the wrong partition even when the final state looks correct.
